spans.content: Detection of Dobrava Hantavirus RNA in
Apodemus Mice in Bulgaria
Iva Christova,1 * Angelina Plyusnina,2 Teodora Gladnishka,1 Nikolay Kalvatchev,1 Iva Trifonova,1
Hristo Dimitrov,3 Vesela Mitkovska,3 Emad Mohareb,4 and Alexander Plyusnin2
1 National Center of Infectious and Parasitic Diseases, Sofia, Bulgaria
2 Department of Virology, Haartman Institute, University of Helsinki, Finland
3 Department of Zoology, University of Plovdiv, Plovdiv, Bulgaria
4 U.S. Naval Medical Research Unit #3, Cairo, Egypt
Several Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic
fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe:
Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV), Puumala,
Saaremaa, Sochi, and Seoul virus. Although
HFRS is endemic in Bulgaria, genome
sequences of hantaviruses have never been
detected in wild rodents. To identify rodent
reservoirs, a total of 691 rodents from
three endemic regions were trapped in 2011–
2012 and screened by TaqMan RT-PCR for
detection of hantaviral genomic RNA.
Partial small (S) and/or large (L)-segment
sequences
were
recovered
from six
Apodemus mice: five of the species A.
flavicollis and one A. agrarius. Phylogenetic
analysis revealed that all
recovered
sequences belonged to DOBV. On the
phylogenetic trees, the novel Bulgarian
hantavirus sequences clustered together
with sequences of established previously
DOBV variants recovered from Bulgarian
HFRS patients and also with variants found
in wild rodents trapped in Slovenia, Greece,
and Slovakia. One of the novel Bulgarian
DOBV S-sequences from A. agrarius was
related closely to DOBV sequences recov-
ered from A. flavicollis, suggesting a
spillover of DOBV from its natural host to
A. agrarius mice. The results of this study
confirmed the circulation of DOBV in wild
rodents in Bulgaria. The complexity of the
epidemiological situation in the Balkans
requires further studies of hantaviruses in
rodent hosts and human HFRS
cases.

INTRODUCTION
Hantaviruses belong to the genus Hantavirus
of the Bunyaviridae family [Plyusnin et al., 2012].
Virions are enveloped, spherical particles with a
diameter of
8 0 { - } 1 1 0 \mathrm { n m }
and have negative-sense,
single-stranded RNA genomes with three segments:
S (small), M (medium), and L (large) [reviewed in
Schmaljohn and Nichol, 2007].
Hantaviruses are maintained in rodents (order
Rodentia, families Muridae and Cricetidae), insecti-
vores (order Lipotyphla, families Soriciodae (shrews)
and Talpidae (moles)) and also in bats (order Chyr-
optera) [Plyusnin and Sironen, 2014]. Hantaviruses
can be transmitted to humans, most commonly
through inhalation of infected rodent excreta. Several
hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal
syndrome (HFRS): Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul
virus (SEOV), Puumala virus (PUUV), Dobrava-Bel-
grade virus (DOBV), Saaremaa (SAAV), Sochi virus
(SOCHV), and Amur-Soochong virus (ASV). Each
hantavirus is associated with a specific natural reser-
voir [reviewed in Schmaljohn and Hjelle, 1997; Plyus-
nin and Sironen, 2014]: PUUV with the bank vole,
Myodes glareolus; DOBV with the yellow-necked field
mouse, Apodemus flavicollis; HTNV and SAAV with
the striped field mouse, Apodemus agrarius (subspe-
cies koreae and agrarius, respectively); SOCHV with
the Black Sea mouse, Apodemus ponticus; ASV with
the Korean field mouse, Apodemus peninsulae; and
SEOV with Norway rats, Rattus norvegicus. There is

HFRS caused by PUUV, DOBV, SAAV, and
SOCHV is widespread in Europe, and the first
SEOV-associated cases have recently been reported
[Jameson et al., 2013, 2012; Mace et al., 2013]. HFRS
cases in China, Korea, and far-eastern Russia are
associated with HTNV, ASV, or SEOV.
HFRS caused by DOBV is endemic in the Balkan
countries and the Alpe-Adrian region. It is usually a
severe illness that presents with hemorrhages, fever,
and acute renal failure that often requires dialysis;
the case-fatality rate may reach
[Avsic-Zupanc
et al., 1999; Jakab et al., 2007]. PUUV and SAAV
cause a milder form of HFRS. PUUV-associated HFRS
is widely distributed in Central and Northern Europe,
the Baltics, the European part of Russia and the Alpe-
Adrian region; it is characterized by fever, back pain,
and renal impairment [Vapalahti et al., 2003].
Located on the Balkan Peninsula, Bulgaria has
been known to be endemic for HFRS since 1953,
when the first cases were identified, based on their
clinical manifestations and epidemiological findings
[reviewed in Kamarinchev et al., 2005]. Annually,
only a few HFRS patients are hospitalized and
registered in Bulgaria. These cases are usually very
severe and often require dialysis. During the past
5 years, a total of 29 laboratory-confirmed HFRS
cases with 2 deaths (fatality rate
) were reported
officially to the Ministry of Health. More than half
were from the districts of Smolyan and Pazardzhik,
while the rest were distributed among the districts of
Blagoevgrad, Plovdiv, Kardzhali, Haskovo, Sliven,
Shumen, and Yambol (Fig. 1).
Based on the known severity of HFRS caused by
DOBV, one can assume that this species is responsi-
ble for the vast majority of hantavirus infections in
hospitalized HFRS patients in Bulgaria, even if other
species cannot be excluded totally. Recently, partial
hantavirus genome sequences were recovered from
three Bulgarian patients with HFRS, and phylogenet-
ic analysis showed that the causative agent in all
three cases was DOBV [Papa and Christova, 2011].
However, genomic RNA of DOBV or other known
European hantaviruses (PUUV, SAAV, SEOV) has
never been detected in wild rodents in Bulgaria. The
aim of the present study was to begin an investiga-
tion of this question by screening rodents collected in
three HFRS-endemic regions for hantaviral genome
sequences, to learn which viruses are in circulation.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Rodent Sampling
Rodents were collected in three districts. Two
districts were selected based on a high incidence of
HFRS: Pazardzhik and Smolyan (South Bulgaria),
while the third had low endemicity: Sliven (East
Bulgaria) (Fig. 1). Sherman live-capture traps were
placed in moist grassy and forest habitats in areas
below
1 0 0 0 \mathrm { m }
above the sea level. Rodent trapping
was performed over 12 months, from May 2011
through April 2012, by 100 traps three consecutive
nights per month. A total number of collected ani-
mals in the three locations were as follows: 294 in
Pazardzhik, 126 in Smolyan, and 271 in Sliven.
Collected rodents were recorded for their species, sex,
and age. Euthanized animals were dissected and
samples of blood, lung, spleen, kidney, liver, and
brain were placed in liquid nitrogen until further
analysis. For investigations, the samples were re-
moved from the liquid nitrogen tanks, sampled, and
transferred to
\mathbf { - } 8 0 ^ { \circ } \dot { \mathbf { C } }
freezers for long-term storage.
Reverse Transcription – Polymerase Chain
Reaction (RT-PCR) for Detection of
Hantaviral Genome

using QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden,
Germany) according to instructions of the manufac-
turer. RNA was then subjected to TaqMan RT-PCR
for identification of conserved region of the S RNA
segment of hantavirus genome. Primers, probes,
and reaction conditions were applied as described
[Kramski et al., 2007]. Reactions were conducted in

RNA from positive lung samples was subjected
to RT-PCR to recover partial hantaviral S and L
segment sequences. Amplification of the partial L
segment sequences was performed with the primers
described earlier [Klempa et al., 2006]. Partial S
segment sequences were amplified with primers:

PCR amplicons were gel-purified using QIA-quick Gel
Extraction kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) and sub-
jected to direct sequencing.
Phylogenetic analysis was done using the PHYLIP
package [Felsenstein, 1993]. Five hundred bootstrap
replicates of the original multiple nucleotide sequence
alignments were generated with the “Seqboot” pro-
gram. Distant matrices prepared using the “Dnadist”
program with a maximum likelihood model for nucle-
otide substitutions were subjected to analysis with
the Neighbor-Joining (NJ) tree-fitting algorithm
(“Neighbor” program). The bootstrap support values
were calculated with the “Consense” program. Relat-
ed hantavirus sequences used for comparison were
recovered from GenBank.

RESULTS
During 2011–2012, a total of 691 small mammals
were trapped in the Pazardzhik, Smolyan, and Sliven
districts of Bulgaria (Fig. 1). Of those, 234 were
identified morphologically as striped field mice (Apo-
demus agrarius), 333 as yellow-necked mice (Apode-
mus flavicollis), 121 as wood mice (Apodemus
sylvaticus) and 3 as bank voles (Myodes glareolus).
Lung samples from each animal were screened using
TaqMan RT-PCR for DOBV and PUUV. Eight ro-
dents were found positive for DOBV and none for
PUUV. Seven of eight DOBV-positive samples origi-
nated from A. flavicollis and one from A. agrarius.
Positive rodents were detected in all three investigat-
ed districts: five in the district of Pazardzhik, two in
the district of Sliven, and one in Smolyan.
Lung samples from all eight positive rodents were
analyzed further by RT-PCR to recover partial hanta-
viral S and L segment sequences. Partial hantaviral S
segment sequences were recovered successfully from six
of the positive rodents: five A. flavicollis (animals #47,
133, 135, and 140 from Pazardzhik and
from
Smolyan) and one A. agrarius (#92 from the locality
Sliven) (Fig. 1). Partial L-segment sequences were also
recovered from rodents #47, 133, and 135. The nucleo-
tide BLAST search revealed the highest level of identity
of the recovered S- and L-sequences to the correspond-
ing sequences of DOBV suggesting involvement of this
particular hantavirus species. The newly described
hantavirus strains were therefore designated as
follows:
 DOBV/Bulgaria_Pazardzhik/Af47/2011,
 DOBV/Bulgaria_Pazardzhik/Af133/2011,
 DOBV/Bulgaria_Pazardzhik/Af135/2011,
 DOBV/Bulgaria_Pazardzhik/Af140/2011,
 DOBV/Bulgaria_Smolyan/Af73/2011, and
 DOBV/Bulgaria_Sliven/Aa92/2011,
Shorter designations for these viruses are: DOBV/
Bulgaria47, DOBV/Bulgaria133, DOBV/Bulgaria135,
DOBV/Bulgaria140, DOBV/Bulgaria73, and DOBV/
Bulgaria92.
Phylogenetic analysis confirmed this conclusion.
The newly recovered Bulgarian hantavirus sequences
clustered together on the phylogenetic trees, with
sequences of the established previously DOBV var-
iants associated with Bulgarian HFRS cases (Bulgar-
iaV36/10, Kardjali 2010, Blagoevgrad 2009, Smolyan
2010, originating from Haskovo, Kardzhali, Blagoev-
grad, and Smolyan, respectively) and also of variants
from wild rodents trapped in Slovenia, Greece, and
Slovakia (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3).

suggests a genetic link between the HFRS case and

Interestingly, strain Bulgaria92 found in A. agrar-

Bulgarian DOBV strains, and also to DOBV strains
from Slovenia, Greece and Slovakia, than to SAAV
strains associated with A. agrarius in Croatia, Slova-
kia, Russia, Denmark, and Estonia.
DISCUSSION
Reliable data on hantavirus circulation in Bulgaria
could be obtained by studying rodent host species.
This report describes the trapping of Apodemus mice
in three HFRS-endemic districts and the first detec-
tion of hantaviral RNA in rodents by RT-PCR,
confirming the circulation of DOBV in Bulgaria.
Unfortunately, due to the chosen trapping locations,
the number of captured M. glareoulus was too small
to learn about the circulation of PUUV in the
country. This investigation is currently on the way.
As expected, Bulgarian DOBV strains form a
compact group, suggesting a relatively recent diversi-
fication point. Some geographical clustering of genetic
variants, for instance of four variants from Pazardz-
hik, can be seen within the group. Phylogenetic
analysis of Bulgarian DOBV sequences showed that
the S segment sequence recovered from one mouse of
the species A. agrarius was closely related to DOBV
sequences recovered from A. flavicollis, suggesting a
spillover of DOBV from its natural host, A. flavicollis,
to A. agrarius.
Morphological misindentification of A. agrarius is
practically impossible due to a number of signs and
especially on a black dorsal medial stripe starting
from interpupillary area and ending to base of tail,
which is not observed in any other member of
Muridae and Cricetidae families of rodents.
Similar spillovers have been reported in Apodemus
mice trapped in Croatia [Plyusnina et al., 2011] and
Germany [Schlegel et al., 2009].
In patients with severe HFRS, DOBV infections
have been confirmed by sequencing of the causative
agents [Papa and Christova, 2011]. Out of 527
hospitalized patients with acute undifferentiated fe-
brile illness, ELISA obtained serological evidence of
current DOBV infection in 8, PUUV infection in 5,
and both DOBV and PUUV in 2 patients. Neutraliza-
tion (PRNT) testing confirmed the hantavirus etiolo-
gy of the febrile illness in 4 patients, who were
reactive only with DOBV [Christova et al., 2013].
In Bosnia and Herzegovina, about half
of
HFRS cases were reported to be caused by DOBV
and
by PUUV [Hukic´ et al., 2011]. Antibodies
against PUUV were also detected in asymptomatic
persons. The simultaneous circulation of DOBV and
PUUV has been described in other Balkan countries
[Avsic-Zupanc et al.,
Papa
and
Antoniadis, 2001; Markotic et al., 2002; Papa
et al., 2006], as well as in Hungary, Czech Republic,
Poland, and Central European Russia [Dzagurova
et al., 2009; Nowakowska et al., 2009; Plyusnina
et al., 2009; Papa et al., 2010]. Four European
hantaviruses (DOBV, SAAV, PUUV, and TULV) have
been detected in rodents in Croatia [Scharninghausen
et al., 2002; Plyusnina et al., 2011].
Taken together, these data illustrate the complexi-
ty of the epidemiological situation for hantaviral
diseases in the Balkans. Further studies are clearly
needed of the circulation of DOBV, PUUV, and other
viruses in natural rodent hosts and their link to
human HFRS cases.
